Chapter 2. The Rise of Bureaucracy and the Loss of Workers’ Power.
After the revolution, the Soviet Union started changing in ways almost no one had expected. Remember all that energy and excitement in the early days? Over time, it faded away, replaced by something entirely different—a force that would come to shape almost every part of life: the bureaucracy.
At first, building up this bureaucracy seemed like a natural step. The country was huge, and the challenges it faced were complicated. Someone had to organize how factories were rebuilt, how food was handed out, how schools and hospitals were run. With the old rulers gone, the new government needed people to keep things moving. A lot of folks stepped into these roles because they truly wanted to help. They believed in the revolution.
But as time passed, the bureaucracy grew into something more than just a way to manage things. It started becoming a class of its own, with special interests and privileges. The people running the state began to see themselves as different from everyone else. They got better food, nicer homes, and more security. Their kids went to special schools, and their opinions seemed to matter a lot more.
For most people, the shift was subtle at first. Maybe a worker would notice that decisions about the factory now came from distant officials, instead of from the workers themselves. Or a teacher might find that classroom lessons were dictated by bureaucrats, not by those who actually taught the kids. That strong feeling of ownership and being part of something bigger—it just started slipping away.
The new leaders said they needed this power for efficiency and stability. They argued that the country was still trying to recover from war, and needed strong leadership. There were threats everywhere, from both outside and within. And after years of chaos, a lot of people agreed—at least for a while. Order sounded tempting.
But that order came at a steep price. The bureaucracy became more and more unaccountable. Criticizing the system? That was risky. People who spoke out could lose their jobs—or face even worse consequences. The soviets, which used to be lively places full of debate, turned into rubber stamps for decisions made somewhere else. Elections lost their meaning, with only officially approved candidates allowed to run.
In private, people complained about this new elite. They saw how officials’ children landed the best jobs, and how the rules always seemed to bend for those with connections. Some folks remembered the early days, when everyone shared in both the hardships and the decisions. Now, it felt like there were two Russias: one for the rulers, and one for everyone else.
Year by year, the bureaucracy’s hold got tighter. It didn’t just run the government—it controlled the economy, the media, even the arts. If you had a fresh idea or wanted to try something new, you usually hit a brick wall. Creativity and initiative gave way to following orders and just blending in. Think about it—the very people who once dreamed of a society run by workers now found themselves ruled by a new class. A class that claimed to speak for them, but rarely actually listened.
This wasn’t just about a few leaders or new policies. It was a deep, fundamental change in what the Soviet state actually was. The revolution had promised democracy, equality, and genuine participation. But now, those things were being pushed aside by hierarchy, privilege, and control. The dream of socialism was slipping away—not because of enemies from outside, but because of changes from within.
